In the Street of Dreams.Chapter 1 : The Train:
The train hummed like a tired lullaby against the rails, each metallic rattle cutting through the silence of the afternoon. I had a book in my lap I wasn’t reading and a life I wasn’t exactly living.

Outside the window, fields blurred into one another — pale yellow merging with silver-gray. Inside, a girl sat across from me, tapping her fingers on her phone, her expression alive with some excitement. Then she said, almost to herself, “What a day it was!”

Her voice startled me — not because it was loud, but because it was so full of light. You could hear the warmth in it, the kind that belongs to people who’ve just lived through something they’ll remember.

I glanced up. She must have been twenty-two or twenty-three, with hair that refused to stay still and eyes that looked like they’d seen a secret. I didn’t know her — not her name, not her story — but I had been a quiet thief of her conversation for the last four stations.

She had been talking on the phone with a friend. Her tone rose and fell like a melody. “He gave me a letter,” she said at one point. “Yes — a love letter!” Then she laughed, that nervous laugh people make when they’re both embarrassed and thrilled.

I didn’t mean to listen, but in a train full of silence, stories travel fast.

Apparently, the letter somehow reached her father’s desk. I could almost imagine that small domestic panic — the blood running cold, the heartbeat caught mid-air. But her father, oblivious, thought it was an academic note and simply handed it back.

I smiled quietly. Another love story, saved by innocence and timing.

Then she read part of the letter aloud, her voice soft and unguarded:

“It’s been nights since sleep has touched my eyes.
Is it you — or the ache of loving you — that keeps me restless?
Tonight, I wait for you at Baran Bock.”

It was clumsy and beautiful in equal measure — exactly the way love should sound. I felt something shift inside me, a strange nostalgia for something that wasn’t even mine.

She spoke again, her words fading into laughter. “No, no, I haven’t gone to meet him yet. Maybe tomorrow,” she said.

Tomorrow. And I, the stranger across the aisle, found myself wondering how it would unfold — her tomorrow, his letter, their meeting. My imagination stitched together scenes: her at the bar, a little nervous; him waiting with a drink gone warm from waiting too long; the air heavy with that electric tension before a confession.

Maybe they’d talk for hours. Maybe they’d fall in love. Maybe they’d part and never meet again. Maybe.

The train kept its rhythm, echoing the pulse of thoughts I couldn’t quiet.

When the next station arrived — Pervouralsk — I stood, still half in her story. I looked back at her once, silently saying goodbye. She caught my eyes and smiled faintly, as if she knew I’d been her secret audience all along.

Maybe that was enough — to be a quiet witness to someone else’s unfolding happiness.

I stepped off the train into the mist. The cold air greeted me like an old acquaintance, wrapping around my coat, filling my lungs with the taste of iron and smoke.

Pervouralsk — the city of mist and stories.
In the Street of Dreams.Chapter 2 : The City of Mist:
They say the mornings here are made of smoke and secrets. Some claim the mist comes from the love and warmth that bind this city together — a visible breath of brotherhood. Others insist it’s just burning weeds in the next district.

I’m not certain either. They say the mist comes from memory — from all the things this city refuses to forget.

It was my second time in Pervouralsk. I had studied here once, long ago. The streets remembered me better than I remembered them. I had come now to begin a job I didn’t plan for — a finance position I never applied for but somehow landed on a sleepy Saturday evening.

The HR manager’s voice on the phone had been cheerful. “Congratulations! We think you’d be perfect for the role.”

“The finance role?” I asked, confused. “I applied for system configurations.”

“Yes,” she said, unfazed, “but you’ll learn fast. And the pay’s good.”

And that was that. Sometimes, fate isn’t poetic — it’s practical.

I stayed with my old college friend, Strive. He lived in a narrow apartment near the old tram line, with too many books and too little furniture. His girlfriend, Olivia, came by often. She worked as a librarian — elegant, curious, and impossibly patient with Strive’s disorderly ways.

Their love story was the kind that begins with an accident.
Strive had written an anonymous letter once — meant for someone else, signed by no one — but it ended up in Olivia’s hands. She read it, smiled, and decided to reply. That was years ago, and they’ve been writing each other ever since — even though they now live together.

Here, they believed every life came pre-written — our loves, our wounds, our fragile triumphs. We were only here to perform what had already chosen us. I had always resisted such fatalism. Yet in this city, doubt found me. Perhaps Olivia was inevitable in Strive’s life. And perhaps I, in my small and passing way, was inevitable in theirs.

“You know,” Strive said one evening as we sat with vodka and old songs playing, “maybe life only begins when we make the wrong delivery.”

I laughed. “You mean like misdelivered letters?”

He nodded. “Or misdelivered dreams.”

The city was quiet that night. Outside the window, the mist thickened, blurring the streetlights into halos.
I thought about that girl on the train again, her half-told story still unfinished in my mind.

Maybe she was from Pervouralsk too.
Maybe somewhere in this fog, her tomorrow had already begun.
In the Street of Dreams.Chapter 3 : Ciaa and the Sea:
There is a street before the old church — narrow, cobbled, lined with birch trees that lean slightly toward each other as if whispering. In winter, the branches catch the snow like lace. In spring, they release it all in one shimmering breath.

At the far end of that street is a bench — my bench — old wood worn smooth by years of solitude. From there, you can see the river curve quietly beneath a low bridge.

Sometimes, it feels as if the sea is opening a door to somewhere else — a distant chorus of forgotten voices drifting in with the light. Then the sky blushes gold before giving itself to stars.

That street had been my refuge during my college years in Pervouralsk.
I spent hours there after lectures, sketching thoughts in the margins of notebooks, smoking until the air around me looked like memory itself. I had grown to know the rhythm of that place — the laughter of children from the nearby playground, the creak of the church gate, the smell of rain when the wind came from the north.

It was on that bench that I first met Ciaa.

She appeared one evening as quietly as dusk. The street was almost empty, and I was counting early stars when she walked up and asked, “Is this seat taken?”

Her accent betrayed her before her words did — soft, lilting, undeniably Spanish.

“No,” I said, shifting slightly. “It’s everyone’s bench. The city just lets me borrow it sometimes.”

She smiled, and in that smile was something familiar — the ease of someone who belongs to the moment entirely.

She introduced herself. “Ciaa,” she said, extending her hand. “Final year, linguistics.”

I shook it. “Same year. Engineering.”

“I’ve seen you in the library,” she said, eyes narrowing playfully. “You always sit near the window but never open your books.”

“I observe,” I said, pretending to be mysterious.

“And what do you observe?”

“The weather,” I said. “And people who ask too many questions.”

She laughed — a real laugh, bright and unguarded — the kind that makes you want to keep talking just to hear it again.

From that evening, the bench belonged to both of us.

We met there often — sometimes by plan, sometimes by coincidence. On weekends, we’d walk to Baron Buchito, a small café at the corner of the street, hidden behind a curtain of ivy. The owner, an old man named Viktor, brewed coffee that could convince even heartbreak to stay a little longer.

Our conversations never really had a point. We spoke about films, her hometown in Spain, the sky, language, and sometimes nothing at all. She told me she came here to study translation, though she believed some feelings could never be translated.

“What word,” she asked one day, “would you use for the feeling of wanting something you already lost?”

I thought for a moment. “Memory,” I said.

She smiled. “That’s a cruel word.”

“It’s the only one I know.”

Before graduation, we decided to take a short trip to Czar Island, a small place off the coast, reachable by an old ferry that coughed more than it sailed. We stayed in a modest inn that smelled of salt and wood polish.

The second evening, we rented a small boat. The sea was glassy and calm. The sun lowered itself into the horizon, spilling gold into the water.

She leaned over the edge, pointing. “Look! A gold koi fish,” she said.

I turned, and indeed — a flash of metallic light rippled beneath the surface.

“They’re rare here,” she said. “You’re lucky to see one.”

“I’m luckier to be here with you,” I said before realizing how hopelessly cinematic that sounded.

She rolled her eyes but smiled. “You sound like a letter.”

“Maybe I am one.”

Then she reached a little too far trying to touch the fish, and in one terrible instant, she slipped.
The boat tilted violently; the sea swallowed her with a gasp.

I froze. For a heartbeat, the world stopped breathing. Then instinct returned — I reached for her, but the water had already blurred her outline into the deep blue.

And then, like a miracle, she surfaced — laughing.
“Are you trying to kill me with your silence?” she said, brushing her wet hair back.

“You nearly gave me a heart attack.”

She climbed back into the boat, drenched and radiant, water dripping from her eyelashes like tears the sea had lent her.

That night, we returned to the inn and had Italian dinner — spaghetti, wine, silence. Outside, the wind moved through the palms like a restless ghost.

She spoke softly after a while. “I’ll be going back to Spain after convocation,” she said. “My father’s business needs me. My brother’s in Madrid now.”

I nodded. “You’ll do great.”

She studied my face. “And you? What do you want?”

I looked at the glass in my hand. “I’m not sure yet. Maybe to find the answer on some bench in some forgotten street.”

She reached across the table, her hand brushing mine for a second — no promises, no declarations. Just a quiet acknowledgment that sometimes, connection doesn’t need permanence to be real.

After convocation, she left.

At first, we exchanged a few letters — short, kind, cautious. Then silence. The kind that doesn’t hurt but settles slowly, like dust.

Years later, I heard she was married — a name mentioned in passing, a photograph seen by someone else. I imagined her somewhere under the Spanish sun, walking down a street that looked nothing like ours, holding a child, smiling the same way.

Sometimes, when nights get too quiet, I wonder if she ever thinks of Pervouralsk, of that street, of the boy who almost lost her to the sea.

The bench remained after she left.
So did I.

I spent many evenings there in those months, speaking to the stars as if they owed me answers. I even named a few, foolish enough to believe that naming something might keep it from leaving.
Maybe, in the end, only the names stay.

Now, years later, I still wonder if those same stars look down and recognize me — older, quieter, still sitting beneath them in memory.
In the Street of Dreams.Chapter 4: The Street of Dreams:
Years passed. I started working as a finance executive — a role that consumed more than it paid. The office walls grew smaller as responsibilities grew larger. The old staff left; the new ones were faster but emptier. I travelled often — from city to city — yet always searching for the same feeling that lived on that quiet street in Pervouralsk.

I bought a small house later. Nastya, a colleague, helped me decorate it — she had a sharp eye for beauty. We even won a carpet in an auction, a royal-looking one with a design once used in imperial courts. I added another EMI to my accounts but didn’t mind. Sometimes beauty deserves debt.

There, at work, I met Vinisa — radiant, confident, brilliant with numbers. We worked together for the Virginia client, shared late-night coffees, and slowly, our meetings moved from conference tables to quiet clubs. We plan to marry soon. She says she loves how I “drift in thoughts even when I’m present.” Maybe she doesn’t yet know how much of me lives in the past.

Ten years later, I returned to Pervouralsk.
The city felt smaller — or perhaps I had outgrown its dimensions. The streets were paved now, the café had changed owners, and the birch trees on the church road had grown heavy with their own histories. The air smelled of rain and old wood, just as it used to.

I arrived on a late autumn afternoon, suitcase in hand, the sky bruised with the first hint of snow. I was supposed to meet my fiancée that evening at a new restaurant by the river, a place everyone said had the best view in town. But instead of calling a cab, I began walking.

Every step along those cobblestones was a conversation with time.
The bakery where I once bought stale bread for dinner had become a florist’s shop. The post office, where I mailed a letter that was never answered, was now painted mint green. And the bench — my bench — still stood at the edge of the street, darkened by years, waiting.

I sat down.

The wind moved through the trees the same way it did in my youth — a rustle, a whisper, a soft insistence that nothing truly stays. The river below looked indifferent.

For a moment, I closed my eyes and imagined the old world sliding back into place — the faint sound of laughter, the weight of notebooks, the scent of coffee and tobacco, and her voice: Is this seat taken?

When I opened my eyes, the bench beside me was empty, but the air felt inhabited.
I found myself smiling, not out of longing, but gratitude — the kind that comes when you finally understand that some absences are just another form of presence.

That night, I went to meet Vinisa. She was waiting at a corner table, her face lit by candlelight, reading something on her phone. When she saw me, she smiled — the kind of smile that belongs to the present, not the past.

“You’re late,” she said softly.

“I took a long detour,” I replied.

“Did you find what you were looking for?”

I hesitated, then nodded. “Yes. A street I once dreamed of. And a version of myself I’d forgotten.”

She reached across the table and took my hand.
Her fingers were warm, steady — quiet proof that life does move forward, even when memory keeps turning back.

Later, back in the hotel, I opened my old journal — the one that once held sketches of the bench, the ferry, the sea. Most of the ink had faded, but the lines still breathed faintly beneath the paper’s yellowing skin.

At the end of the book, on an empty page, I wrote:

Some stories don’t end;
they simply dissolve into the air,
carried in every breath we take.
Some faces remain, not to unsettle us,
but to whisper that we once loved deeply enough to remember.
Perhaps we never live them — perhaps they live us,
and every city keeps a part of you — just as you keep a part of it.

Outside, the first snow began to fall — soft, hesitant flakes melting against the glass. The streetlights flickered, the night hummed faintly with the sound of passing trains, and somewhere in that silence, I heard the sea again.

Not as an echo of loss — but as a promise that everything once loved returns in another form.

The next morning, I left Pervouralsk again.
But this time, I didn’t look back.

Some places, once seen twice, don’t remain stories —
they become part of your blood, your breath, your rhythm.

And when the train pulled away, I realized the story I’d been chasing all these years had already found its ending.

It wasn’t in the girl, the bench, or the sea.
The mist followed me a while, then disappeared.
But I knew, with a calm that felt like joy, that the city would keep dreaming me long after I was gone.
In the Street of Dreams.Summary:
The narrator travels by train, lost in routine and quiet detachment from life. On the journey, he overhears a young woman excitedly recounting her first love letter — a small, beautiful moment that stirs in him a forgotten tenderness and curiosity about love and fate.

He arrives in Pervouralsk, a mist-covered city tied deeply to his memories. Years ago, he studied there, stayed with his friend Strive and Strive’s lover Olivia — a couple whose romance began from a misdelivered letter. In this city, the narrator once believed in chance, destiny, and quiet magic.

There, he met Ciaa, a Spanish classmate, on an old bench by a river. Their connection was warm, effortless, and unspoken — a friendship touched by almost-love. They shared quiet afternoons, small adventures, and a near-tragic moment at sea that revealed how deeply he cared for her. But life separated them; she returned to Spain, and they faded into silence. She eventually built her life elsewhere, while he continued drifting, holding onto memories like pressed flowers.

Years pass. He works, buys a house, finds companionship with Vinisa — a grounded, intelligent woman who loves him, though parts of him remain tethered to the past.

Returning to Pervouralsk a decade later, he walks through a city that has changed yet remembers him. He sits again at the old bench, not longing anymore, but honoring what once was. Time has turned old ache into quiet gratitude — for youth, love, places that shape us, and moments that never fully leave.

He meets Vinisa with a peaceful heart. The past no longer anchors him; it completes him. Leaving the city again, he feels not loss but closure. The mist stays behind, holding his younger self — and he departs knowing the story has ended exactly as it should.
In the Street of Dreams.Philosophical Takeaways:
1. Not every meaningful connection is meant to stay.

Some people enter our lives not to remain, but to awaken a part of us — then leave us changed, softened, more awake.

2. Beauty does not always ask for permanence.

Moments can be brief and still eternal. A shared bench, a laugh in the wind, a letter read aloud… meaning does not require forever.

3. Life unfolds not through grand plans, but accidents.

A misdelivered letter, a random train seat, a stranger’s smile — fate often moves through tiny, unnoticed hinges.

4. Naming things is an act of love.

We name what we fear losing — because sometimes the name is all that survives the passing.

6. The self we chase is often the self we once were.

We return to places not to find someone else, but to find versions of ourselves we left behind.

8. Closure is not an event — it's a realization.

When the heart finally whispers, It was beautiful. And it’s okay that it ended.

10. Some absences are a form of presence.

Those we once loved never truly leave — they walk beside us in memory, shaping how we see the world.

11. The world is often absurd — and still, we live tenderly.

Life does not always make sense, yet we keep hoping, loving, remembering — and that quiet persistence is its own meaning.
In the Street of Dreams.One-Line Essence: Life is not about keeping everything you love — it’s about learning to live fully with what remains, and tenderly with what doesn’t.

A Subway At AIIMS.Chapter 1: The Quiet Beginning:
The school bell started ringing, pulling me out of the half-sleep I had been floating in during the last few lectures. All I wanted was to get out of the classroom. Not because home was calling me, but because a cricket match was waiting right after school. A group of ten friends had fixed it in advance, and no matter how hot the sun burned, our dedication at that age didn’t care. Heat, sweat, exhaustion — nothing mattered.

For the past few days, though, I had been losing match after match. I knew I needed more practice, but evening tuition classes stole whatever time and energy I had left. By the time I finished dinner at night, I could barely keep my eyes open long enough to imagine playing better the next day. My days ended with stress, and mornings started like a battle I had to prepare for again and again.

There was a girl in my class who always sat on the front bench. Light brown hair, a round face, timid eyes — but sharp enough to make me feel like I had done something wrong every time she looked at me. Sometimes she stared at me with such intensity that it felt like she was trying to kill me with her eyes. Typical first-bencher: studious, disciplined, the teacher’s favourite.

We had never talked.
And honestly, with the way she looked at me, I wasn’t sure I ever could.

Some classmates once joked that she liked me. But with those death stares, I could barely stand in front of her without my heart racing — I’ve never been good with fast bowlers anyway, so I did what I always do: let that ball go untouched.

Years passed. I completed my 12th, and like every batch that eventually scatters, all of us moved to different cities, different careers, different lives. Barely a few stayed in touch. And with the personality I have, I hardly manage to keep people close for long. Sooner or later, I get consumed by the chaos of my own world, leaving contacts buried under time.

I chose engineering and did well in it. Won medals too. My quiet, boring personality turned out to be good for something — it gave me plenty of time to focus on my career. After graduation, I got a software development job at an MNC. I poured myself into my work the same way I once poured myself into cricket, and in a few years, that dedication paid off.

Last year, I met a girl online through someone I knew. I messaged her casually, and slowly we became good friends. We played games, joked around, kept in touch from time to time — a simple bond, but a pleasant one. And only after a while did I discover the truth: she was the same girl who used to scare me in school — Supriya.

Recently, she had been away for a while. I wondered what was going on and finally messaged her. She replied that she wasn’t doing well in life.

I grew curious. I kept asking my usual never-ending questions. Her replies were slow, distant. I thought maybe she was busy with someone else, maybe dating, maybe just tired. I never imagined anything serious. I don’t know why, but her voice, her name, her way of talking had always felt different to me — something I had never experienced before.

And then one day, she called me suddenly.

Her voice was weak, trembling. She told me her reports had shown Stage 3 abdominal cancer — a rare type, difficult to treat. My mind went blank. I couldn’t understand how or why it happened. But life never gives reasons for everything.

She sounded exhausted. I could feel her struggling even to speak. I quickly asked for the hospital details before she hung up, telling me the doctor had arrived.

After the call, I sat silently, shocked and helpless.
All I could think about — day and night — was going to see her.
As soon as possible.

Something inside me shifted in that moment.
And I didn’t know then… this was just the beginning.
A Subway At AIIMS.Chapter 2: Not a Date, But the First One:
When I walked into the ICU, I froze. It was the first time I saw her sleeping — really saw her after years. Something inside me shifted. I had never felt anything like it before. She looked familiar, almost painfully familiar, like someone I had known forever even though I was seeing her for the first time in my conscious memory.

Her face was pale, but there was a strange warmth in it, as if she had been waiting for me long before I even arrived. I caught myself wondering how beautiful her eyes might be when they opened.

While I was lost in that thought, I noticed her mother sitting on the small sofa beside the bed. Alone. Quiet. The kind of silence that tells you life is a battle you often fight by yourself. A part of me — I don’t know from where — wished I could be a small part of that battle.

The air in that room was heavy. Heavy enough that I felt breathless, unable to speak or ask anything. It felt like time had paused, like I was standing inside a moment I wasn’t prepared for. If I could have taken her pain into away, I would have done it without a second thought.

I finally walked closer. Her mother gestured for me to sit. I handed her the water bottle lying lifeless on the table. She took a sip, but even that felt too heavy for her. She didn’t know me well, yet her eyes held a strange familiarity — like she had met a version of me somewhere before.

When I hugged her, I whispered, “Everything is going to be okay.” Even though inside, I was just as helpless as she was.

A single tear fell from her eye and landed directly on my chest, right above my heart. I swear my heartbeat stumbled for a second. But I stayed strong — or at least pretended to.

After a while, she slowly opened her eyes. And just as I had imagined — they were beautiful. A little red from weakness, but shining. Like her soul hadn’t given up.

“Finally you came to see me,” she said softly.

“Did you think I wouldn’t?” I replied.

She looked away. “It’s hard to expect anything from people now. We’ve only known each other online. Why would someone care for me in this state?”

For a moment, I couldn’t speak. The world really has changed that much — people don’t expect care anymore.

She waited patiently for my answer.

To lighten the moment, I said, “Actually, I feel like I’m not even from this world. Maybe from some other planet.”

She laughed — the same laugh I’d heard during our voice calls. Loud, free, and strangely comforting. Her smile was the most weirdly beautiful thing I had seen in a long time. I kept staring, which made her instantly hide it, thinking maybe her condition made me uncomfortable.

I shook my head lightly. “A smile like yours shouldn’t be hidden. The world would feel empty without it.”

She relaxed a little.

Then she asked, “Have you been missing me these days?”

How could I tell her that the sky I stared at every night made me more restless than I thought I am, thinking about her!

I said, “What is there to miss when you’re right in front of me now?”

Her lips trembled slightly. “That day might not always come… you know.”

I smiled softly. “One of the gods is my friend. I’ll ask her to make this forever.”

She blinked at me. “Will they listen to you?”

“They always do,” I said. “It’s not my first time asking them. They always do.”

She smiled — a fragile, hopeful smile. Even if it wouldn’t last forever, at least she saw someone wishing for her in a world where most people only wish for themselves.

She might have liked me — I knew that. But distance had created small gaps between us. Even then, from the very beginning, I had felt something for her. And I was smart enough to know love isn’t something that happens in a moment or a dream.

But then why did this feel so different?

I had brought flowers and a chocolate for her.

“These are for you,” I said.

She smiled. “Thank you… flowers are okay, but chocolates aren’t allowed.”

“Oh,” I said. “Then I’ll have to find someone else for them.”

She burst out laughing. “Seriously! You’ll never change.”

“Oh, so you don’t like me the way I am?” I teased.

She shook her head softly. “You’re the best soul I’ve met. Maybe God wanted me to meet you before I go.”

My heart stopped for a moment.

“Now that I’ve met you,” I said, “do you think I’ll let you go?”

She felt awkward — her mother was still in the room — so I quickly corrected myself.

“I mean… aunty won’t let you go, right?”

She smiled a bit, and the moment turned normal again.

I wanted to kiss her forehead — just a small kiss — but it felt too soon, especially with her mother sitting right there. I don’t usually care about anything when I’m in love, but honestly, love has tested me enough to make me question my own philosophies.

The hospital was average — clean but small. Her father worked as a bank employee in West Delhi. Their earnings were enough for a decent life, but big hospitals charge in a way that doesn’t just fail to save the one admitted… they slowly kill the ones paying. I wasn’t very different. Just another middle-class guy working as a software developer. I earned okay, but my ambitions kept growing, often making even the sky feel low.

Then the doctor walked in.

“That’s enough for today. She needs rest. She has chemo tomorrow.”

Her eyes instantly filled with fear — and hope, both at the same time. Hope that I’d come again. Fear that I might not.

I held her hands gently and said, “Everything will be fine. I told you… I’ll come again.”

She nodded.

As I walked out, her mother accompanied me to the exit.

I looked at her and asked, “Is there anything I can do?”

“We don’t need anything right now, she will be moved to AIIMS tomorrow for better treatment, you can visit often” she said softly. “But you coming today… it made her truly happy. We haven’t seen her smile like that in a long time.”

I nodded. “I will.”

And with that, I left the hospital for the day — carrying her tear, her smile, and her fear inside my chest, like they all belonged to me.
A Subway At AIIMS.Chapter 3: The Unknown Storyteller:
Days passed, and she was getting a little better, though it was hard to say anything with certainty. I hadn’t been able to visit her for a week, but I stayed in touch with her mother, asking about every little change, every bit of progress.

It was Saturday — a day that didn’t demand much from me. I decided I had to see her. I brought flowers again, but no chocolate this time. Instead, I picked up a juice, hoping this one wouldn’t require a “Plan B” recipient.

I took an auto to Noida City Centre Metro Station, switched between a few lines, and finally reached AIIMS.

Above the main road near the station, there’s a long pedestrian subway bridge — about the height of a five-storey building. From up there, you can see one of the busiest stretches of Delhi, a never-ending river of vehicles flowing day and night.

I had spent hours on that bridge before… just standing, watching the chaos below. It calmed me in a strange way — people rushing, people waiting, people arguing with autorickshaw drivers, people booking cabs — everyone going somewhere.

And then there was me, standing alone, not rushing anywhere.

That’s where I met Prakash.

We bumped into each other randomly. A thin guy, maybe in his early twenties, with a smile that somehow refused to fade. He told me he had lost both his parents when he was eight. He ran a small tea stall nearby and sometimes sat on the subway bridge when he got tired.

There was a quiet honesty in his voice.

He spoke about how his father suffered from a liver disease, how they waited endlessly for a bed at AIIMS. He talked about long waiting lists, endless queues of patients, and how only people with contacts or influence managed to get treatment on time. His father eventually got a bed — but too late. Too late for recovery, and too expensive for hope.

The sadness in his eyes wasn’t the kind that asked for pity. It was the kind that had learned to live with itself.

I felt the heaviness of his story.

In return, I told him about Supriya — her health, her struggle, my fear.

Despite his own pain, he patted my back and said,
“Things will get better. People say there is a God above the clouds… and a pure heart like yours will get his attention.”

I didn’t know whether he believed what he said.
I didn’t know whether I believed it either.
But somehow, his words calmed me.

It was almost 6 in the evening. The bridge was empty except for the two of us. I turned for a moment, then asked him where his tea stall was — I told him I’d visit for a cup of tea.

I turned back.

He was gone.

Just like that.

He hadn’t walked away — I would’ve heard footsteps.
There were no exits nearby.
No other people on the bridge.

He had simply… disappeared.

A cold shiver ran down my spine. But I was getting late, so I rushed toward the hospital.

She looked better that day.

Her room was 604. She was alone, sitting by the window, watching kids play in the garden below. The moment she saw me, her eyes brightened.

“Mr. Busy Guy, you’re back,” she teased.

“Yes,” I smiled. “Where’s your mother today?”

“She’ll be back in an hour. Went home to get food for me.”

“You could’ve told me. I know how to cook too. I would’ve made something for you.”

She laughed softly. “Really? You want to make me more sick?”

“You doubt my cooking skills?”

“Of course. I’ve never tasted anything you’ve made.”

I shrugged. “I never got the chance to cook for you.”

She smiled. “Next time, bring rajma. That’s my favourite. You know how to make it?”

“In theory, yes,” I said. “My spices go up and down sometimes… but there are tutorials for emergencies.”

She gave me a playful stare. “So you’ll experiment your cooking skills on me?”

“Why not?”

We laughed together, just looking at each other — a calm moment in the middle of all the chaos.

“I brought juice today,” I said.

“Oh? You’ve really been thinking about what to bring, haven’t you?”

“Yes,” I said quietly. “Anything to make my friend feel better.”

“I don’t know why,” she whispered, “but hearing that… I already feel better.”

“I’m glad my visits help,” I said. “Honestly, I could stay here all night.”

“And office? Isn’t work hectic?” she asked.

“It’s been years doing this job. I’ll manage.”

“So sweet of you,” she said. “But not needed. My mother will be here.”

“Okay,” I smiled. “But I’ll always be a thought away.”

She rolled her eyes. “Don’t use your flirty lines again. What will you even do after impressing me now?”

“Oh… so you’re not impressed yet? Looks like I’ll have to work a little harder now.”

She laughed. “Very funny. You never miss a chance.”

“If it’s for you, then I won’t.”

A little later, her mother returned. She was genuinely happy to see me again. I greeted her and stepped out so Supriya could eat and rest.

It was around 8 PM. I thought of grabbing a cup of tea and maybe finding Prakash’s stall. I searched nearby, asked around, but no one had heard of him. No tea stall matched his description. No one even knew anyone named Prakash in that area.

When I mentioned meeting him on the subway bridge, one man said:

“Everything that happens on that subway isn’t real. That bridge has seen and absorbed so much pain… it creates its own stories, its own people.”

I stood there, stunned.

Was Prakash even real?
Who was he?
Where did he disappear in seconds?
Was his story true… or just another echo from that strange bridge?

With those questions swirling in my mind, I headed back home.
A Subway At AIIMS.Chapter 4: The End of the Story?:
A week later, while I was getting ready for work, my phone rang. It was Supriya’s mother. She rarely called, and never without a reason. The moment I saw her name, something inside me tightened.

I picked up immediately.

Her voice was shaking.
“Something has gone wrong… the doctors said her condition suddenly collapsed. They… they don’t know how long she has.”

I couldn’t respond for a few seconds.

“But she was doing better,” I said softly. “She was improving.”

“I don’t know what happened,” she whispered. “They’re trying, but her body isn’t responding anymore.”

My heart sank.

“I’m coming right now,” I said, already grabbing my keys.

The ride to the hospital felt endless. I don’t remember the roads or the traffic — just the fear that kept building in my chest.

When I reached her floor, her mother was waiting in the corridor. Her hands were trembling, her eyes swollen from crying.

“She’s inside,” she said quietly.

I walked into the room.

Supriya was lying still, looking more fragile than I had ever seen her. Her face looked calm, but in a way that scared me. The machines were beeping in slow, uneven intervals.

I pulled a chair closer and held her hand. It was cold.

“Hey,” I whispered, “I’m here.”

She didn’t respond. Her breathing was shallow and slow. The pauses between each breath felt longer and heavier.

“I thought you were getting better,” I whispered. “There was still so much you had to say… and I still had so much to ask.”

Her mother stood behind me, quietly crying.

The doctor came in, checked the monitor, and sighed.

“I’m sorry,” he said softly. “Her body isn’t responding anymore.”

He left the room.

Time felt like it had stopped. I kept talking to her even though she couldn’t hear me. Her breathing grew weaker.

Then it slowed.

And then it stopped.

A nurse came in, checked her, and looked at us gently.

“She’s gone.”

The words didn’t feel real. It was like the world had shifted and refused to settle back.

A tear rolled down my face before I even realized it. It felt like something inside me had cracked open.

Her mother sank into a chair, crying, and I held her because there was nothing else to do.

Later, we took Supriya home. Her room still felt like her — the books, the neatly folded scarf, the little things she used every day. Everything felt heavier than before.

The next morning, after the rituals, people came to offer condolences and left. And slowly, over the hours, it felt like Supriya drifted from this world to wherever she was meant to go.

When her ashes settled, I whispered to myself,
“I hope you’re free now. And if there’s something beyond this… I hope you can still hear me.”

I don’t know if she could.

But I wanted to believe she did.

There was a song of backstreet boys I loved years ago, one that slipped out of my memory with time. I didn’t understand it back then. But today, every word feels like it was written for me.

“Show me the meaning of being lonely

Is this the feeling I need to walk with?

Tell me why I can't be there where you are

There's something missing in my heart

Life goes on as it never ends

Eyes of stone observe the trends

They never say, forever gaze, if only

Beauty roams to an endless love

There's no control, are you with me now?

Walk with me and maybe

Nights of light so soon become

Wild and free, I could feel the sun

Your every wish will be done.

They tell me..”
A Subway At AIIMS.Chapter 5: The Never-Ending Love:
Few years have passed.

Life has changed in ways I never imagined, yet some things have stayed exactly the same — untouched, almost sacred. Once every year, on the same quiet afternoon, I visit Supriya’s mother. We sit together on her small balcony, two cups of tea slowly growing cold between us. She tells me stories about her daughter — the tiny memories, the habits, the moments she still holds close. And every time, I listen with the same stillness, as though hearing them for the very first time.

In those moments, neither of us tries to fill the silence.
We simply let Supriya be there with us, the way she always has.

My own life kept moving too. I got married last year. My wife understands more than she ever says. She knows a part of me is tied to a chapter she can never enter, and she never tries to.

We have a daughter now.

Her name is Supriya.

It wasn’t a decision made from memory or longing. It just felt gentle… natural. A quiet way of honoring the girl who once changed something inside me. My wife agreed to the name before I even finished saying it. Maybe she understood without needing words.

My daughter is nothing like the Supriya I knew, but sometimes, when she laughs suddenly or thinks deeply with her head slightly tilted, something inside me pauses — not with sadness, but with gratitude. Life returns warmth to places we once thought would always remain cold.

I still have a photograph of Supriya — one I took quietly in the hospital. It has stayed in my suitcase all these years, hidden from everyone. Some nights, I open the suitcase and talk to her, asking how she’s doing in her own world now, don't know which world she belongs to now.

Maybe she isn’t in this world anymore… but she’s with me, and she’ll stay alive as long as I do.
A Subway At AIIMS.Summary:
“A Subway at AIIMS” follows the quiet, reflective journey of a young man who reconnects—almost accidentally—with an old classmate, Supriya, years after school. What starts as casual online friendship becomes a profound emotional bond when he discovers she is battling a rare and aggressive cancer.

Their connection deepens through small conversations, fragile laughter, and unspoken feelings shared in the hospital’s silence. As he visits her in AIIMS, he finds himself confronting truths about care, love, helplessness, and the strange ways two lives can collide at the wrong time, yet still mean everything.

He also meets Prakash — a mysterious stranger on a subway bridge outside AIIMS — whose sudden disappearance leaves him questioning fate, destiny, and the unseen forces surrounding places filled with so much human suffering.

When Supriya’s condition suddenly collapses, he rushes to be with her in her final moments. Her death leaves behind a quiet but permanent imprint on him — a grief that softens rather than hardens him.

Ten years later, his life has moved forward: a marriage, a daughter, a new chapter. But a part of him still keeps Supriya alive — in memories, in conversations with her photograph hidden in his suitcase, and in the understanding that some people remain with us even after they’ve gone.
He visits her mother every year, sharing silence, tea, and the warmth of remembering someone who mattered.

Supriya’s story doesn’t end with her death; it becomes part of how he lives.
A Subway At AIIMS.Philisophical Takeaways:
1. Some stories end early, but their meaning doesn’t. Supriya’s life was short, but it shaped him for decades. Not all love stays, but all love changes us.

2. People don’t leave — they shift form inside us. She exists now as memory, warmth, tenderness, and the part of him that knows how to care deeply.

3. Love isn’t defined by duration, but by depth. He met her late, lost her early, and still found a lifetime’s worth of emotion in between.

4. Some strangers appear only to guide us. Prakash — real or not — represented those inexplicable moments in life where help arrives from places we never understand.

5. Life continues, but it never erases what mattered. Time doesn’t heal everything. It just teaches us how to live with tenderness instead of pain.

6. The world repeats the same stories — but we live them differently. Just like the opening quote, the book shows how love, loss, and memory happen to everyone — but the experience is uniquely ours.
